Exemplary embodiments described herein relate to pool cleaners configured to remove debris from water through the use of a plurality of cyclonic flows. In such embodiments, water and entrained debris may be drawn into the pool cleaner and directed through one or more separation regions where cyclonic motion assists in separating debris from the water. The use of multiple cyclonic flows may improve debris collection efficiency, reduce clogging, and help maintain consistent hydraulic performance during operation.

Some embodiments include removable, replaceable, or modular components that facilitate assembly, servicing, repair, or customization of the pool cleaner. For example, a pool cleaner may include a removable impeller subassembly, a particle separator assembly, a roller drive gear box, a roller latch, and removable wheels. These components may be configured so that a user or service technician can access, remove, replace, or clean them without requiring extensive disassembly of the entire cleaner.

Certain embodiments are directed specifically to check valves for debris canisters. Such check valves may help retain collected debris within a canister when water flow stops, when the cleaner is removed from the pool, or when the debris canister is being emptied. Other embodiments are directed to roller latches that secure rollers to pool cleaners. These latches may allow rollers to be held firmly in place during use while also permitting convenient removal for cleaning, replacement, or maintenance.

Exemplary filter media may include embossments or raised features that define or create flow channels for water passing through the pool cleaner. These embossments can help maintain spacing, reduce blockage, improve water distribution across the filter media, and enhance filtration performance. By providing defined flow paths, the filter media may allow water to move more efficiently while still capturing debris.

Additional embodiments include various structural, electrical, and mechanical improvements for pool cleaners and related equipment. These may include alternative pump motor engagement arrangements, contoured potted power board assemblies, kickstands for supporting or positioning the cleaner, pool cleaner caddies for transport and storage, and improved roller assemblies. Together, these features may contribute to improved durability, ease of use, serviceability, performance, and overall functionality of pool cleaning systems.
outputs.L4:
The described pool cleaner systems and accessories incorporate a range of innovations intended to improve cleaning performance, simplify maintenance, enhance mobility, and make the overall user experience more convenient. In several embodiments, debris removal and filtration are improved through the use of cyclonic flow paths that help separate debris from water more efficiently. These flow arrangements may direct water and debris into a chamber in a manner that promotes swirling or vortex-like movement, causing heavier debris to move away from the main water stream while filtered water continues through the cleaner. This can reduce clogging, improve suction consistency, and extend the time between filter cleanings.

The systems also include removable subassemblies that allow key components to be accessed, serviced, replaced, or cleaned with less effort. For example, filter units, debris chambers, drive assemblies, or other internal modules may be configured to be detached from the cleaner body without requiring extensive disassembly. This modular approach can reduce maintenance time and allow a user to replace only the affected component rather than the entire cleaner. In some configurations, valves are used to control water flow, regulate suction, or redirect debris-laden water through selected passages. Such valves may improve hydraulic performance and help the cleaner adapt to different operating conditions.

Additional features are directed to secure assembly and retention of components during operation. Locking handles and latch mechanisms may be provided to ensure that covers, filter housings, debris containers, or other removable parts remain firmly in place while the cleaner is moving through the pool. These locking structures may also be designed for intuitive release, allowing users to open or remove components quickly when cleaning or maintenance is required. Modular gearboxes may further improve serviceability by allowing drive components to be installed, removed, or replaced as self-contained units. This can be especially useful for maintaining traction, steering, and movement reliability over time.

The filtration media used in the cleaner may include embossed or otherwise textured filter surfaces. These structures can increase the effective filtration area, improve flow distribution, and help capture fine particles while resisting collapse or blockage. By shaping the filter media, the cleaner may maintain better water throughput and debris collection efficiency. Some embodiments also include alternative motor engagement arrangements that allow motors to connect with pumps, drive elements, or other mechanical systems in different ways. These arrangements may improve power transfer, reduce wear, simplify assembly, or allow a common motor platform to be used in multiple cleaner designs.

Power management and electrical component placement are also addressed. Contoured power boards may be shaped to fit within limited internal spaces of the cleaner body or accessory housing. By conforming to available contours, these boards can make more efficient use of space and may improve packaging, cooling, or protection from water intrusion. Such designs can support more compact cleaner bodies while still accommodating the electronics needed for navigation, motor control, charging, or system monitoring.

The innovations further extend to usability features outside the cleaner itself. Kickstands may be provided to support the cleaner or a related component in a stable position when removed from the pool, making storage, inspection, or maintenance easier. Caddies may be used to transport and store the cleaner, power supply, cables, hoses, or accessories. These caddies can improve portability and organization, particularly for larger robotic or powered cleaner systems. Removable wheels may also be included to allow worn or damaged wheels to be replaced easily, or to permit different wheel types to be installed for different pool surfaces or operating conditions.

Together, these embodiments provide a comprehensive set of improvements for pool cleaner systems. The cyclonic flow and enhanced filter media improve debris separation and filtration performance. Removable subassemblies, modular gearboxes, valves, latches, and locking handles make the cleaner easier to assemble, maintain, and service while ensuring that components remain secure during use. Alternative motor engagements and contoured power boards improve mechanical and electrical integration. Finally, kickstands, caddies, and removable wheels enhance handling, transport, storage, and long-term usability. Collectively, these features contribute to more efficient cleaning, reduced maintenance burden, improved reliability, and a more user-friendly pool cleaning system.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style summary paragraph describing exemplary embodiments of an invention relating to robotic pool cleaners and associated components.
counterfactuals.output: Exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure relate to robotic pool cleaners and associated components, systems, and methods for cleaning submerged surfaces of a swimming pool or spa. In certain embodiments, a robotic pool cleaner includes a housing, a drive assembly configured to propel the cleaner along a pool surface, one or more cleaning elements such as brushes or scrubbers, a debris intake in fluid communication with a debris collection chamber, and a filtration assembly configured to separate debris from water drawn through the cleaner by a pump or impeller. The cleaner may further include one or more sensors, including waterline, orientation, proximity, pressure, inertial, optical, or flow sensors, and a controller configured to determine cleaning patterns, adjust drive operation, detect obstructions, identify walls, floors, steps, or waterlines, and optimize cleaning performance based on sensed operating conditions. Associated components may include removable filter cartridges, modular drive tracks or wheels, replaceable brush assemblies, docking or retrieval devices, charging interfaces, power supplies, buoyancy elements, sealing arrangements, cable management features, and user-control interfaces, including wireless communication modules and mobile-application connectivity. In some embodiments, the robotic pool cleaner is configured to operate autonomously or semi-autonomously, perform selected cleaning cycles, climb pool walls, traverse irregular surfaces, conserve energy, and provide status, maintenance, or diagnostic information to a user, thereby improving reliability, cleaning efficiency, debris capture, ease of maintenance, and overall operation of the pool-cleaning system.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the disclosed pool cleaner inventions, including cyclonic debris removal, removable impeller assemblies, check valves, filter media, roller assemblies, power supplies, kickstands, caddies, and removable wheels.
counterfactuals.output:
The disclosed pool cleaner inventions relate to improvements in robotic or suction-type swimming pool cleaners, focusing on debris handling, serviceability, mobility, storage, and power management. Key concepts include:

- **Cyclonic debris removal:**  
  The cleaner may use cyclonic or vortex flow to separate debris from water. Water and debris enter a chamber where rotational flow causes heavier debris to move outward and collect, improving filtration efficiency and reducing clogging of the main filter.

- **Removable impeller assemblies:**  
  The cleaner can include an impeller or pump assembly that is removable as a unit. This allows easier access for cleaning tangled hair, leaves, or other debris, and simplifies repair or replacement without disassembling the entire cleaner.

- **Check valves:**  
  One-way valves may be used in the cleaner’s flow path to prevent debris or dirty water from flowing backward out of the cleaner when the pump stops or when the cleaner is lifted from the pool. This helps retain collected debris inside the cleaner.

- **Filter media and debris containers:**  
  The inventions include removable filter cartridges, baskets, bags, or other filter media designed to trap fine and coarse debris. These filters may be easy to remove, rinse, and reinstall, and may be arranged to work with cyclonic separation or other pre-separation systems.

- **Roller assemblies:**  
  Roller or brush assemblies may be provided to improve traction, scrub pool surfaces, guide the cleaner along walls or floors, and help move debris toward an intake. The rollers may be removable or replaceable for maintenance.

- **Power supplies:**  
  The cleaner systems may include specialized power supplies for operating pumps, motors, controls, or robotic drive systems. These power supplies may be configured for safe poolside use, may include control electronics, and may support detachable power connections.

- **Kickstands:**  
  A kickstand or support feature may be provided on the cleaner or associated equipment to hold the device in a stable upright or service position. This can make it easier to remove filters, clean components, or store the cleaner after use.

- **Caddies:**  
  A transport caddy may be included for moving and storing the cleaner and related equipment, such as the power supply and cable. The caddy may include wheels, handles, brackets, or storage areas that organize the cleaner system and improve portability.

- **Removable wheels:**  
  The cleaner may have wheels that can be removed or replaced without major disassembly. This allows users to service worn wheels, change wheel types for different pool surfaces, or more easily access internal components.

Overall, the inventions aim to make pool cleaners more efficient at collecting debris, easier to maintain, more reliable in retaining debris, and more convenient to transport, store, and service.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

The cleaner may include one or more brushes, rollers, tracks, wheels, impellers, suction structures, filtration elements, or directional control components configured to improve cleaning of pool floors, walls, waterlines, steps, corners, and other surfaces.

Accessories may include docking stations, charging assemblies, retrieval devices, caddies, replacement filter cartridges, debris bags, wall-climbing aids, hose attachments, skimmer adapters, brush attachments, and maintenance tools.

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal patent language, describe exemplary embodiments directed to pool cleaners, debris canisters, particle separators, roller latches, pump motor engagements, power supplies, and caddies.
counterfactuals.output:
Exemplary embodiments disclosed herein relate generally to swimming pool and spa cleaning systems and, more particularly, to autonomous and/or robotic pool cleaners, removable debris collection assemblies, particle separation structures, roller retention mechanisms, pump and motor engagement arrangements, power delivery assemblies, and transport or storage caddies therefor.

In one exemplary embodiment, a pool cleaner comprises a housing configured for travel along a submerged surface of a pool, at least one inlet formed in or adjacent a lower portion of the housing, at least one outlet in fluid communication with the inlet, and a pump assembly configured to induce a flow of pool water through the cleaner. The cleaner may include one or more drive members, such as wheels, tracks, rollers, brushes, or combinations thereof, arranged to support and propel the cleaner over a pool floor, wall, step, bench, waterline region, or other surface. A controller may be operatively coupled to at least one drive motor and/or pump motor to implement a cleaning cycle, navigation routine, wall-climbing routine, waterline-scrubbing routine, or debris-collection routine.

In certain embodiments, the pool cleaner includes a debris canister removably received within a canister compartment of the cleaner housing. The debris canister may comprise a frame, a handle, one or more porous filtration walls, a debris inlet port, and a lid or access door movable between open and closed positions. The canister may be insertable into and removable from the cleaner from a top side, front side, rear side, or lateral side of the housing. In some embodiments, the canister includes a sealing surface configured to engage a corresponding sealing surface of the cleaner housing to inhibit bypass flow around the canister. The canister may further include a latch, detent, cam, magnetic retention feature, resilient tab, or other retention element configured to releasably secure the canister in an installed position.

In additional embodiments, the debris canister includes a particle separator arranged upstream, downstream, or within a filtration region of the canister. The particle separator may be configured to separate relatively large debris, relatively dense debris, sand, silt, leaves, hair, insects, or other particulate matter from the water stream before the water stream passes through one or more filter elements. In one form, the particle separator comprises a cyclonic, vortex, tangential-flow, centrifugal, inertial, baffle-based, screen-based, or gravity-assisted separator. In another form, the separator comprises a chamber having an inlet oriented to impart swirl to the incoming flow and a collection region positioned to receive separated debris. The separator may reduce clogging of a filter screen, increase effective filtration capacity, or maintain pump performance during a cleaning cycle.

In some embodiments, the particle separator is integrally formed with the debris canister. In other embodiments, the particle separator is a removable cartridge, insert, or module selectively mountable to the canister. The separator may include one or more vanes, ramps, guide surfaces, nozzles, flow directors, perforated walls, mesh elements, or deflectors configured to alter the velocity, direction, or distribution of fluid flow. The separator may be cleanable by opening a lid, removing a cap, flushing the separator, or withdrawing a debris cup from the canister.

In certain embodiments, the pool cleaner includes one or more rollers arranged adjacent a lower surface, forward region, rearward region, or side region of the housing. A roller may comprise a cylindrical body, brush body, foam body, elastomeric sleeve, bristle assembly, ribbed surface, or traction-enhancing member. The roller may be mounted on a shaft, axle, spindle, hub, or bearing support. In exemplary embodiments, the cleaner includes a roller latch configured to releasably retain the roller relative to the housing. The roller latch may be movable between a locked position, in which the roller is retained for operation, and an unlocked position, in which the roller is removable for cleaning, replacement, or maintenance.

In one embodiment, the roller latch comprises a pivotable latch arm having a hook portion configured to engage a roller shaft or bearing block. In another embodiment, the latch comprises a sliding lock member movable along a guide track to capture or release an end of the roller. In still another embodiment, the latch includes a resilient clip, bayonet coupling, quarter-turn lock, over-center cam, spring-biased pawl, rotatable retainer, or tool-less release member. The latch may be accessible from an exterior of the cleaner housing and may include a gripping portion, tab, button, lever, or textured actuator to facilitate operation by a user. The latch may be configured to resist unintended release during operation of the cleaner in water.

In further embodiments, a pump motor engagement arrangement is provided for coupling a pump motor to a pump impeller, pump volute, pump cartridge, or pump housing. The pump motor may be mounted in a dry compartment, sealed motor chamber, removable motor module, or flooded motor region. The engagement arrangement may comprise a mechanical coupling, magnetic coupling, spline interface, keyed shaft, bayonet mount, threaded engagement, snap-fit connection, or compression seal arrangement. In some embodiments, the pump motor is configured to engage a pump cartridge when the cartridge is inserted into the cleaner housing, thereby establishing both mechanical drive communication and fluid communication.

In one exemplary embodiment, the pump motor includes an output shaft configured to mate with an impeller hub. The output shaft and impeller hub may include complementary alignment features to ensure proper assembly. In another embodiment, the pump motor and impeller are magnetically coupled through a sealed barrier, thereby permitting torque transfer while maintaining electrical components isolated from pool water. In yet another embodiment, the pump motor is included in a removable service module that may be withdrawn from the cleaner housing without disassembly of the entire cleaner. Electrical contacts, seals, locating ribs, guide rails, or latch members may be provided to facilitate repeatable installation and removal.

In some embodiments, the pool cleaner includes a power supply configured to provide electrical power to the cleaner. The power supply may comprise an external power unit connected to the cleaner by a cable, a rechargeable battery carried by the cleaner, an inductive charging assembly, a docking station, a solar-assisted charging component, or combinations thereof. The power supply may include a transformer, rectifier, inverter, power conditioning circuit, battery management system, charge controller, over-current protection, ground fault protection, thermal protection, communication interface, or user control interface.

In embodiments employing a tethered configuration, a cable may extend between the cleaner and a power supply positioned outside the pool. The cable may include one or more conductors for power delivery and/or data communication. A swivel, strain relief, buoyancy element, connector, or detachable coupler may be provided to reduce tangling, permit service, or improve cleaner mobility. In embodiments employing an onboard battery, the cleaner may include a watertight battery compartment and charging contacts, inductive coils, or a sealed charging port. The controller may monitor state of charge and adjust cleaning behavior based on available energy.

In further embodiments, the power supply includes a user interface configured to receive one or more inputs corresponding to a cleaning mode, cleaning duration, delay start, floor-only operation, floor-and-wall operation, waterline operation, filter status, canister-full indication, or diagnostic mode. The user interface may include buttons, touch-sensitive regions, indicator lights, display screens, audible indicators, wireless communication circuitry, or network connectivity. The power supply may communicate with the pool cleaner through the power cable, wirelessly, optically, acoustically, or by another communication link.

In additional exemplary embodiments, a caddy is provided for transporting, storing, charging, or supporting the pool cleaner and associated components. The caddy may comprise a frame, a handle, one or more wheels, a cleaner support region, a cable storage region, and a power supply mounting region. The cleaner support region may include one or more cradles, saddles, hooks, rails, shelves, posts, or retention members configured to support the cleaner in an elevated or inclined position. The caddy may be configured to drain water from the cleaner after removal from the pool.

In certain embodiments, the caddy includes a receptacle or bracket for receiving the debris canister, particle separator, filter panels, brushes, rollers, or other removable components. The caddy may further include a cord wrap, cable reel, swivel mount, power supply shelf, battery charging dock, or accessory tray. In some embodiments, the caddy includes a charging interface configured to electrically connect with the pool cleaner when the cleaner is positioned on the caddy. Such charging interface may comprise conductive contacts, an inductive charging coil, a magnetic alignment feature, a guided docking connector, or a sealed electrical coupling.

In one embodiment, the caddy frame includes a lower support platform and an upper handle portion joined by upright members. Wheels may be mounted near a lower rear region of the frame so that the caddy may be tilted and rolled by a user. The cleaner may be supported such that one or more rollers, brushes, tracks, or wheels are spaced from the ground to reduce deformation during storage. The caddy may also include retention straps, latches, projections, or recesses configured to inhibit movement of the cleaner during transport.

In some embodiments, the pool cleaner, debris canister, particle separator, roller latch, pump motor engagement, power supply, and caddy are configured as an integrated system. For example, the cleaner may include a top-loading debris canister having an integral cyclonic separator, a tool-less roller latch for removal of a front brush roller, a magnetically coupled pump motor isolated from pool water, an external low-voltage power supply with programmable cleaning modes, and a wheeled caddy configured to carry both the cleaner and the power supply. In another example, the cleaner may include an onboard rechargeable battery and may be docked on a caddy having an inductive charging station and storage locations for interchangeable filter cartridges.

In accordance with additional embodiments, a method of operating a pool cleaning system comprises placing a pool cleaner in a pool, supplying power to a pump motor and at least one drive motor, drawing pool water and debris through an inlet into a debris canister, separating at least a portion of debris within a particle separator, filtering the water through one or more filter media, discharging filtered water from the cleaner, and propelling the cleaner along a pool surface. The method may further comprise removing the cleaner from the pool, actuating a canister latch to withdraw the debris canister, emptying the canister, actuating a roller latch to remove a roller for cleaning or replacement, and positioning the cleaner on a caddy for storage or charging.

In accordance with still further embodiments, a method of servicing a pool cleaner comprises releasing a roller latch, removing a roller from a roller support, cleaning or replacing the roller, reinstalling the roller, and actuating the roller latch to retain the roller in an operational position. The method may further comprise removing a debris canister, separating a particle separator module from the canister, flushing debris from the separator, reinstalling the separator in the canister, and reinstalling the canister in the cleaner housing. The pump motor engagement may permit removal of a pump cartridge or motor module independently of the canister or drive assembly.

The foregoing exemplary embodiments may be implemented individually or in any suitable combination. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be incorporated into other embodiments unless technically inconsistent. The scope of the disclosed subject matter is not limited to the particular arrangements, shapes, materials, or configurations described, and encompasses variations and equivalents suitable for use in pool cleaning systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise “exemplary embodiments are directed to…” section for inventions involving pool cleaners with cyclonic flow debris separation and modular serviceable components.
counterfactuals.output:
Exemplary embodiments are directed to a pool cleaner configured to separate debris from water using cyclonic flow. In some embodiments, the pool cleaner includes a cleaner body, a fluid inlet, a fluid outlet, and a debris-separation chamber arranged to induce a cyclonic flow path that urges debris toward a collection region while permitting filtered water to exit the cleaner.

Exemplary embodiments are also directed to a debris collection module removably coupled to the pool cleaner body. The debris collection module may include a cyclonic separator, a debris receptacle, and one or more sealing interfaces configured to allow removal, emptying, cleaning, or replacement of the module without disassembly of the cleaner body.

Exemplary embodiments are further directed to modular serviceable components for a pool cleaner, including one or more removable cyclonic separator cartridges, filter elements, inlet assemblies, outlet assemblies, impellers, drive modules, sensor modules, or debris bins. The modular components may be configured for tool-less attachment and detachment, guided alignment, and fluid sealing when installed.

In certain embodiments, the pool cleaner includes a modular flow path in which incoming debris-laden water is directed tangentially into a separation chamber to generate cyclonic motion. Larger debris may be separated by centrifugal action and collected in a debris container, while finer debris may be captured by a downstream filter element. The debris container and filter element may be independently removable for servicing.

Exemplary embodiments are additionally directed to methods of operating and servicing a pool cleaner. The methods may include drawing pool water into the cleaner, generating cyclonic flow to separate debris, collecting separated debris in a removable module, discharging cleaned water from the cleaner, and removing one or more modular components for emptying, cleaning, maintenance, or replacement.
